subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Forces and Motion
subtitle: Forces, motion, Newton's laws, friction, gravity, energy, and fair-test investigations.
description: A physical science revision pack covering how forces explain, predict, and change the motion of objects. Students practise key vocabulary, calculations, Newton's laws, balanced and unbalanced forces, friction, gravity, energy, data interpretation, and fair-test reasoning.

data.sourcePassage: Motion describes how an object's position changes over time. To describe motion clearly, scientists compare the object with a reference point, such as a road, start line, tree, or bus seat. A passenger on a moving bus is moving compared with the road, but not compared with the seat. Speed tells how fast an object moves and is calculated by dividing distance by time. Velocity includes both speed and direction, so 5 m/s east and 5 m/s west are different velocities. Acceleration means any change in velocity, including speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.

questions.question: What does motion describe?
questions.modelAnswer: Motion describes how an object's position changes over time.

questions.question: Which formula calculates speed?
questions.modelAnswer: Speed is distance divided by time.

questions.question: Why can a passenger be moving compared with the road but not compared with the bus seat?
questions.modelAnswer: Motion depends on the reference point. The passenger changes position compared with the road, but stays in the same position compared with the seat.

questions.question: Which situation is acceleration?
options: a car turning a curve at constant speed
a book resting on a desk
questions.modelAnswer: A car turning a curve at constant speed is accelerating because direction changes.

questions.question: Explain why direction matters when describing velocity.
questions.modelAnswer: Velocity includes direction, so two objects with the same speed can have different velocities if they move in different directions.

data.sourcePassage: Usually, more than one force acts on an object at the same time. Net force is the overall force after all forces are combined. Forces in the same direction are added, while forces in opposite directions are subtracted. If two students push a cart to the right with 20 N and 15 N, the net force is 35 N right. If a box is pushed right with 30 N while friction pushes left with 10 N, the net force is 20 N right. Balanced forces have a net force of 0 N and do not change motion. Unbalanced forces cause acceleration.

questions.question: What is net force?
questions.modelAnswer: Net force is the overall force after all forces are combined.

questions.question: What is the net force when 20 N right and 15 N right act on the same cart?
questions.modelAnswer: The net force is 35 N right.

questions.question: What is the net force when 30 N acts right and 10 N friction acts left?
questions.modelAnswer: The net force is 20 N right.

questions.question: Why can a book resting on a table have forces acting on it but no change in motion?
questions.modelAnswer: Gravity pulls down and the normal force pushes up. These forces are equal and opposite, so the net force is 0 N and the book's motion does not change.

questions.question: How do you know whether an object will accelerate?
questions.modelAnswer: Identify the forces and combine them. If the net force is not 0 N, the forces are unbalanced and the object accelerates in the direction of the net force.

data.sourcePassage: Newton's first law says that an object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion keeps moving at the same velocity unless acted on by an unbalanced force. This is the law of inertia. Newton's second law explains that force, mass, and acceleration are related: F = ma. Greater net force causes greater acceleration if mass stays the same, while greater mass causes less acceleration if net force stays the same. Newton's third law says that for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. These force pairs act on different objects, so they do not cancel each other.

questions.question: Which law is called the law of inertia?
questions.modelAnswer: Newton's first law is called the law of inertia.

questions.question: What formula represents Newton's second law?
questions.modelAnswer: Newton's second law is represented by F = ma.

questions.question: Why does an empty cart accelerate more than a full cart when pushed with the same force?
questions.modelAnswer: The empty cart has less mass and less inertia, so the same net force causes greater acceleration.

questions.question: Which example best shows Newton's third law?
options: a swimmer pushes water backward and the water pushes the swimmer forward
a book rests still on a desk
a toy car travels at constant speed
a ball has more mass than a feather
questions.modelAnswer: The swimmer and water example shows equal and opposite forces acting on different objects.

questions.question: Explain why action-reaction forces do not cancel each other.
questions.modelAnswer: They are equal and opposite, but they act on different objects. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object.

data.sourcePassage: Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces that touch. It can be helpful when shoes grip the ground, bike brakes stop wheels, or a pencil writes on paper. It can also cause machine parts to wear out and transfer energy as heat. Gravity is an attractive force between objects with mass. Earth's gravity pulls objects downward, and weight is the force of gravity on an object. Mass is different because it measures the amount of matter. Motion is also connected with energy. Moving objects have kinetic energy, while objects can store potential energy because of position or shape.

questions.question: What does friction oppose?
questions.modelAnswer: Friction opposes motion between surfaces that touch.

questions.question: Which is a helpful use of friction?
questions.modelAnswer: Shoes gripping the ground is a helpful use of friction.

questions.question: How are mass and weight different?
questions.modelAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, while weight is the force of gravity on that object.

questions.question: Which object has kinetic energy?
options: a stopped car with no motion
questions.modelAnswer: A moving bike has kinetic energy because kinetic energy is energy of motion.

questions.question: Why can friction be both helpful and a problem?
questions.modelAnswer: Friction is helpful when it gives grip or helps objects stop, but it can be a problem when it wears parts out, slows motion, or transfers useful energy as heat.

data.sourcePassage: Forces and motion explain many real-world safety and engineering problems. During a sudden stop, a passenger's body tends to keep moving forward because of inertia. A seat belt applies a force that slows the passenger more safely. A bike helmet works differently: it increases the time over which the head slows down, helping reduce the force during a crash. Engineers test helmets by dropping head models, collecting force data, comparing materials, and improving designs. In lab investigations, students use evidence from data tables. If the same toy car travels farthest on smooth tile and shortest on carpet, the evidence suggests carpet has more friction.

questions.question: Why does a passenger's body tend to keep moving forward during a sudden stop?
questions.modelAnswer: The passenger's body tends to keep moving forward because of inertia.

questions.question: What does a bike helmet increase during a crash?
options: the stopping time for the head
questions.modelAnswer: A bike helmet increases the stopping time for the head.

questions.question: What evidence would support the claim that carpet has more friction than tile?
questions.modelAnswer: If the same toy car travels a much shorter distance on carpet than on tile, that data supports the claim that carpet has more friction.

questions.question: How do engineers use evidence when designing safer helmets?
questions.modelAnswer: They test helmet designs, collect force data, compare materials, and improve the design based on results.

questions.question: Connect inertia, force, and safety in the example of seat belts.
questions.modelAnswer: Inertia makes the passenger keep moving when the car stops. The seat belt applies a force to change the passenger's motion and slow them in a controlled, safer way.
